heading: Separate travel from time at the base
intro: Begin with the exact start and end of the package. A day listed in a brochure can include getting to the lodge, settling in or returning to a gateway, so it should not automatically count as a full day of outings. Ask for the sequence for your dates and identify which arrangements you book separately. Put each overnight on a simple calendar and mark the proposed activity periods around it. This makes two similarly named packages easier to compare. A shorter arrival journey might leave different usable time than another proposal, but you need the written details to assess that. Keep unconfirmed connections visible and avoid using another operator’s timetable to fill the gaps in your own plan.
points: Where does this package begin and end?
How is arrival and departure time used?
Which connections do we arrange separately?

heading: Use three days for a focused introduction
intro: A three-day option is worth examining when your travel window is limited and your main interest fits the proposed schedule. Ask how many nights are included rather than reading the day count as a night count. For example, Tucán Lodge labels its short option three days/two nights; that example does not establish the terms of every other provider. Look for the full activity period between arrival and departure, then ask what changes compared with the longer program. If an activity you care about is absent, decide whether the shorter stay still meets your priorities. Compare the complete journey, including travel outside the package, before judging whether the option is convenient for your group. Keep the confirmed itinerary beside the quote.
points: How many lodge nights are included?
Which outings fit the actual three-day schedule?
What is omitted compared with the longer option?

heading: Compare four days as a useful middle option
intro: A four-day proposal gives you a useful middle point for comparing the short and longer options from the same property. Count the nights and inspect where full activity periods fall. Ask what changes from the three-day version: an additional outing, another setting or a different allocation of time. Those differences matter more than adding one to the package title. Read the activity demands alongside the sequence so the schedule fits your group, and ask what arrangements can be adjusted for the booking. A published example is helpful for understanding the structure, but the confirmed proposal should establish the details for your dates. Compare the complete total and exclusions with the other options before deciding whether the added time meets your priorities.
points: Which full activity periods are included?
What changes from the shorter program?
How do activity demands fit our group?

heading: See what a fifth day adds
intro: Use the five-day proposal to ask what an additional night actually contributes. It might mean another outing, returning to a setting or more space between activities, depending on the program. Ask the provider to show the difference in the schedule rather than assuming every longer option offers all three. If quiet observation, photography or simply spending more time at the base matters to you, explain that interest and compare the proposed allocation of time. The bird image here records a particular encounter; more time does not guarantee the same encounter for you. Read guiding and habitat alongside duration. Once you understand the changes, weigh the extra night against its complete cost and the time available for the rest of your Ecuador journey.
points: What changes with the additional night?
How much time is available for observation and rest?
Which outings are included or optional?

heading: Choose a pace you will enjoy
intro: Describe a few priorities instead of asking for every possible activity. A group interested in photography might value time to remain in one setting, while another may prefer a mix of outings and time at the base. Ask how the proposed program supports those interests and which parts are shared with other travellers. Discuss walking and boarding requirements early, especially if they influence how much you want to do in a day. An itinerary can look impressive on paper while leaving little room for the pace you prefer. Review the sequence together and ask which adjustments are possible, without assuming a private guide or unlimited flexibility. Choose the duration that supports a coherent experience for the people travelling, rather than treating a long checklist as the goal.
points: How does the program support our main interests?
Which outings are shared or private?
What adjustments are possible for the agreed booking?

heading: Connect the stay to the rest of Ecuador
intro: Work backwards from the next part of your journey and make the return arrangements visible. Confirm the provider’s endpoint and the onward transport you book separately, including who is responsible for each connection. Ask what happens if an arrangement changes and keep the relevant contact details with the written plan. Do the same for travel before the package so the lodge stay does not become an isolated block on the calendar. You may decide to keep time between travel segments; choose that through the actual connections rather than an invented universal buffer. Check current official advice for every gateway and transfer route. The duration decision is complete only when the nights, activities and adjoining journeys fit together in a plan you understand.
points: Where does the return journey finish?
How are changes communicated for the actual booking?
